Path is how far above (+) or below (−) your line of sight the bullet is, for the zero you picked (the circle in its zero box). Adjust is how far to dial up from the zero your scope is set to. Wind drift is for a full-value crosswind; hold or dial into the wind.

True up velocity

Shot at long range and needed a different dial than the table shows? Enter what actually hit, and it works out the muzzle velocity that matches, so the table and dope card line up with your real hits. Use a distance well past your zero (300 yd or more) and a solid group.

Dope card & reticle

Tap a distance on the card to see it on the reticle.

A small card to tape to your stock or keep in your range bag. It uses the zero your scope is set to, the conditions above and the crosswind you entered. Up is how far to dial up; wind is how far to hold or dial into the wind. The reticle is a plain one in your scope's units (tap Change how it looks to make it like yours), or a picture of your own reticle if you've added one to the gun's scope under Gear & Ranges › Optics. The plain one isn't any brand's design, so count the marks on yours. Put the target on the dot. It adds spin drift when the bullet length and twist are filled in; until then a note above the card says so.

Saved ranges

Pick one of your saved ranges to see the dial and wind for each of its targets with this profile and the conditions above. Add and change ranges under Gear & Ranges › Ranges.

Getting started

A one-minute walk through the basics.

Signing in

The admin makes your account and gives you a temporary password. The first time you sign in you'll choose your own. To change it later, tap More at the bottom right, then Account (on a computer, Account is at the top right). Want a different name shown (on shared loads, box photos and the greeting on Home)? Ask the admin; they can change it with Edit name on the Admin page.

Colors

To use metric, go to More › Account › Units and tap Metric. Distances then show in metres, velocities in m/s, bullet drop, drift and group sizes in centimetres, cartridge sizes (COAL, case and bullet length, twist, barrel) in millimetres, energy in joules, temperatures in °C, wind in km/h, altitude in metres and bulk powder in kilograms. Bullet weights and powder charges stay in grains. Nothing you've saved changes, only how it's shown, so you can switch back and forth. The setting follows your account to your other devices, and the Excel and PDF exports and printed targets use it too. In metric, the range table and dope card step in whole metres, the wind brackets are 10, 20 and 30 km/h, and a zero typed in metres stays that many metres. A zero you set in yards shows its metric equivalent (100 yd shows as 91 m). The help on this page uses imperial units.

On a phone, the bar along the bottom shows four tabs and More. To choose which four, and their order, go to More › Account › Phone tab bar and tap Choose the tabs: tick In the bar for up to four (Home, Shooting, Reloading, Gear & Ranges, Tools and How to Use) and drag them into order. The rest are under More. A computer always shows every tab along the top.

Pick a color theme under More › Account › Theme: Range (the original), Olive Drab, Flat Dark Earth, Blued Steel, Blaze Orange, Plum, Lavender or Red Night. Under the themes, pick Woodland camo or Digital camo for a faint camo pattern behind the page in your theme's colors, or Plain for none. Each one can follow your phone's light/dark setting or stay light or dark. Red Night is always dark red-on-black, so it won't wreck your night vision. Your choice follows your account to your other devices.

Getting around

Range Book opens on Home: buttons to start a range day or a new load, anything that needs attention (components running low, a barrel near the end of its life, a gun due for cleaning), your rounds fired this month and year, your recent range trips, Recent reloading (the loads you've worked on lately), your Most used guns (your favorites first, then the guns with the most rounds, with their photos; up to six, and All guns › for the rest), and Built in Library: how many bullets, cartridges, powders, factory ammo, scopes and primers are built in. Tap a number to open that list, or Open Library › for the Library page under Reloading › Reference, which lists everything built in with its count and shows the bullets by maker. On a computer, Recent range trips and Recent reloading sit side by side, Most used guns gets its own column on the right (on a narrower screen like a tablet it goes under them), and Built in Library runs across the bottom; on a phone the cards are one under another. Arrange Home at the bottom puts the cards in your order and turns off the ones you don't need. Tap Range Book at the top to get back to it. On a phone the sections are along the bottom: Home, Shooting, Reloading, Gear & Ranges and More (How to Use, Admin, Account and Sign out). On a computer they're across the top. At the top of Reloading, Loads | Components switches between your recipes and your components; at the top of Shooting, Profiles | Range log does the same, and Tools opens to a tile for each calculator. When you open a load, profile or gun, ‹ Loads, ‹ Profiles or ‹ Guns above its name takes you back to the list. On a phone or tablet you can also swipe in from the left edge of the screen to go back up a level (from a range trip to the profile's trips, from a load or profile to the list, from a gun to your guns), and the phone's own Back button does the same. Each tab (Home, Shooting, Reloading, Gear & Ranges, Tools and Account) has a Tour button at the top right (▶ on a phone) that walks you through what that tab does, card by card; it may open the SAMPLE load to show you around, but it doesn't change anything. Next to it, Help (? on a phone) opens How to Use at the part about what you're looking at; tap ‹ Back to… at the bottom to go back where you were. On Shooting, Reloading, Gear & Ranges and Tools, the cards also have a small ⓘ next to their title: tap it for a quick how-to for that card, and More in How to Use › for the full story.

When a note or this page mentions another part of Range Book, the name is an underlined link in your theme's color, like Gear & Ranges › Ranges. Tap it to go straight there. A path with › shows where it is, so you can also find it yourself.

Paste or drop a picture. On a computer you don't have to hunt for the file: copy a picture (or take a screenshot) and press Ctrl+V (⌘V on a Mac), or drag a picture or file from your desktop onto the page. It goes to the + Add button on the screen you're on, just like picking it with that button: a gun's or scope's photos, a reticle picture, target photos, box photos, documents, or a file to import. When a screen has more than one, drop it on the card you want (it gets a dashed outline). Pasting while you're typing in a box pastes text as usual.

Arrange Home at the bottom of Home lets you put its cards in your own order (drag ⠿, or use ▲ and ▼ on a computer) and turn off the ones you don't need. Usual order puts everything back. It's saved to your account, so every phone and computer shows the same Home.

The Range log (the Range log button on Home, or Shooting › Range log) lists every day you've shot, newest first and grouped by month: your range trips, plus each day you shot groups for a Reloading load (one entry per load per day, with the number of groups, the charges, rounds and the best group). At the top are this year's days at the range, rounds, trips and load-development days, and your best group of the year. Tap Range trips or Load development to show just one kind, pick a gun to see only its days, or search by place, load or date. Tap an entry to open that trip, or that load's groups.

Start a range day on Home asks which gun you're shooting, then what you're shooting through it: one of your Shooting profiles, ammunition from your inventory, or factory ammo from the catalog that you don't have yet (it lists the catalog loads for the gun's cartridge, and the search box finds any other). Picking ammo makes the Shooting profile for that gun the first time, and a catalog pick is added to your Ammunition list with no rounds on hand, so you can count what you shoot from it. It opens a new range trip dated today and, if your phone shares its location, fills in the temperature and wind. You can also start one from a gun's page.

Tap a card's title (Point-blank range, Range table, Groups, Photos, the sections of this How to Use page and so on) to fold it out of the way; tap it again to open it. Range Book remembers which cards you closed on that phone or computer. Long lists (loads, profiles, guns, optics, suppressors, inventory, range trips, components) get a Search box at the top: type part of a name, cartridge, place or date. On Gear & Ranges it also finds a serial number, with or without its dashes and spaces. When you delete something (a load, profile, gun, trip, photo, group, component or ammunition), a note at the bottom says so with an Undo button for a few seconds. If you close Range Book and come back within 12 hours, it opens where you left off.

Add it to your iPhone home screen

Open this page in Safari, tap the Share button, then Add to Home Screen. It gets its own icon and opens full screen.

When the server has a new version, the app tells you with a banner that floats at the bottom of the screen (just above the tabs on a phone), so you see it wherever you are on the page: tap Reload now to switch to it (you land back where you were). It checks when the app opens, when you switch back to Range Book and every minute while it's open, so there's no need to close the app.

Changed something on another phone or computer? In the home-screen app, scroll to the very top of the page and pull down until it says Release to refresh, then let go. Anything you were still typing is saved first, then the app reloads with the newest data and puts you back where you were. (In a browser tab, use the browser's own refresh.)

Where your data lives

Everything saves to your account automatically, so it follows you to any phone or computer you sign in on.

No signal at the range

Open Range Book once on your phone through its https:// address while you have a signal. After that it opens even with no signal, showing your loads and photos as of the last time it synced. Anything you change or add (shots, groups, photos, measurements) is kept on the phone, and a yellow Offline tag at the top shows how many changes are waiting. They upload by themselves when you get a signal again. Don't sign out while changes are waiting, or they're lost.

Using more than one phone or computer

You can change things on your phone at the range (even with no signal) and on your computer at home, and nothing gets lost when the phone syncs. Range Book combines the two piece by piece: if the phone changed a load's velocity and the computer changed its name, you get both; a gun, ammo, trip or load added on either one is kept; something deleted on one stays deleted unless the other changed it later. Only when both changed the very same thing (the same box on the same load, say) does one win, and it's the newer edit, by the time you made it. A device that's been open a while shows the other's changes after you pull to refresh or reopen the app.

Guest mode

If the admin has turned it on, the sign-in page has a Try it as a guest button. Guests can use everything, but nothing is saved: it's all gone when the page is closed or reloaded. Guests can print the Printable targets too, so someone trying Range Book can print one and try Live target or measuring a photo.

Feedback and ideas: found something wrong, or have an idea? More › Account › Feedback and ideas opens your own email app (or GitHub) addressed to the person who makes Range Book, with the version filled in. Nothing is sent from this server. You can also write to hello@rangebook.org directly.

Printing from the home-screen app on an iPhone or iPad: a PDF (a target, a trip report or an export) opens a small panel instead of a new page. Tap Print or save…, then Print (or Save to Files) in the share sheet. In a browser, PDFs open in a new tab as before.

Shooting

The Shooting tab is the trajectory calculator plus your range trips and printable targets.

Pick or make a profile

A profile is one gun and the ammo you shoot in it, with its zero, scope and conditions: everything the calculator needs. (On Reloading, a load is still a load.) The Shooting tab (the trajectory calculator and your range trips) opens to a list of your profiles, grouped by cartridge and sorted by name (long-range profiles are tagged, and so are profiles whose ammo is marked Subsonic). Set a profile's Cartridge at the top of its inputs to move it to that group. Tap one to open it, and tap ‹ Profiles to go back. Tap the star on a profile (or Add to favorites at the top of its inputs) to make it a favorite: favorites are listed first, under ★ Favorites, and come first when Start a range day asks what you're shooting. Put them in your own order: press and hold one (or drag it with a mouse) and drag it up or down the Favorites list. To add your own, tap + New profile. It starts blank: pick the gun and ammo (or type the numbers). Leave Profile name blank and it's named after the gun and ammo, like "Tikka T3x - Hornady 6.5 Creedmoor 143 gr ELD-X", and it follows if you change either; type a name to use your own. On the Bullet path card, Short charts to 200 yd, Medium to 400 yd and Long to 1,000 yd (and the range table to 2,000 yd). Your profiles are saved to your account. To remove a profile, open it and tap Delete profile at the very bottom (Undo brings it back). That works for the sample profile too, which also has Reset to defaults if you've changed it and want the original back.

A new account's Shooting list starts with a single SAMPLE · 6.5 Creedmoor profile, and on a new Range Book the first account also gets a matching worked-up ladder on Reloading. They're made up to show how things fit together, and they're marked with a warning: don't load or shoot anything from them without checking a current load manual. Delete them whenever you like.

Fill in the fields

  • Gun: pick one of your guns from Gear & Ranges and its sight height fills in. Edit beside it opens that gun on Gear & Ranges, with a ‹ Back to button to return to the profile. Profiles sent over from Reloading come with the gun already picked. If you change the gun's sight height on Gear & Ranges, the calculator follows unless you've typed in your own.
  • Ammunition: tap it to pick your own factory or reloaded ammo, or a load from the factory catalog. Fill in the Cartridge first and the list shows only ammo for that cartridge (and ammo that's safe in it, like 223 Remington for a 5.56 gun); tap Show all cartridges at the top of the list to see everything. The bullet weight, BC, diameter and length fill in from the ammo. If the ammo has no bullet length, Range Book uses its reloading recipe's, or the length saved on its bullet under Components.
  • Bullet weight: from the ammo box.
  • Muzzle velocity: the box number comes from a test barrel and is often 50–150 fps faster than your gun. A chronograph reading is best.
  • Velocity measured at and Temp sensitivity (optional): powder burns faster when it's warm, so a load is faster in summer than in winter. Enter the temperature your velocity was measured at and how many fps it changes for every 10°F (often 5–20 fps), and the calculator adjusts the velocity for the temperature on the Conditions card. Under the profile's Range trips, a Velocity and temperature chart can work out the sensitivity from your own trips (it needs trips with an average velocity and temperatures at least 10°F apart); tap Use … in the calculator to fill it in. When you use a trip's average as the muzzle velocity, its temperature is saved as "measured at".
  • Ballistic coefficient (G1): on the box or the bullet maker's website. Use the G1 number, not G7.
  • Bullet diameter: e.g. .224, .243, .277, .308, .338, .357. Used for sectional density and the form-factor check below the inputs. The path itself comes from the BC.
  • Zeros: the boxes at the bottom of the Bullet path card, under the chart. The first one (purple) is the point-blank zero, worked out from the target size in the Point-blank range card. Type up to three more distances to compare, each with its own color; leave one blank to hide it. Tap the circle on the zero your scope is set to: the Range table and Dope card say at the top which zero they're using.
  • Scope zero: tap the circle in the zero box your scope is actually set to (that box gets a highlighted border). The range table's MOA and MIL columns and the dope card are based on it.
  • Conditions (its own card, under Inputs): hot weather and high altitude make bullets drop less. For the wind, enter its speed and the o'clock it comes from (12 is straight at you, 3 from the right, 9 from the left); the calculator works out how much of it pushes the bullet sideways and which way to hold. Head and tail winds barely matter and aren't counted.
  • Shot angle: for shooting up or down hill, enter the angle (either way, it's the same). Only part of the drop counts at an angle, so you hold or dial less than on level ground; the table, chart and dope card all use it. Leave it blank for level shots.
  • Range table columns: under the range table, tick Adjust (MOA), Adjust (MIL) and Wind to choose which of those columns to show (Wind includes the wind brackets and spin drift). Range, velocity, energy, time and the path are always there. Your choice is remembered on that phone or computer. When you pick a gun whose scope has MOA or MIL turrets, the matching Adjust column is ticked and the other unticked (you can still tick both), and the wind column switches to MIL when only MIL is shown. Drag the bar under the table to make it taller or shorter, like the chart; double-tap it to reset.
  • Spin drift is in the range table's Wind columns (in inches, to the right) and in the Spin R column of the dope card, Field mode and a saved range's dope, and it's added to the reticle's hold. It's counted from your zero, like Coriolis. It needs the gun's twist and the bullet length. Until both are filled in, a Spin drift is off note shows above the range table and the dope card; tap Enter it to jump to the missing box (or Edit the ammo when the bullet comes from your ammo).
  • Wind brackets: turn this on to add 5, 10 and 15 mph full-value wind holds to the range table and dope card (and Field mode), so you can hold for whatever the wind is doing without changing the inputs.

Reading the results

  • Near, Far and Top: shown in each zero box. Where each path rises through 0 (near) and comes back down through it (far).
  • Highest point: how far above your line of sight each path climbs, and at what range. It's listed as Top in each zero box under the chart. Handy for knowing how high you'll hit at mid ranges, or for a point-blank zero.
  • Path (in): inches above (+) or below (−) your line of sight, for the zero you picked with the circle in its zero box (pick a different one and the column follows). Negative means hold or dial up.
  • Adjust (MOA / MIL): how far to dial up from the zero your scope is set to.
  • Wind: drift for a full-value crosswind. Hold or dial into the wind.

Point-blank range

The Point-blank range card (the Point-blank link at the top) works out the best zero for holding dead on. Enter the size of what you're shooting at, or tap 4" varmint, 6" deer or 8" elk. It finds the zero that keeps the bullet within half that size above or below your line of sight for as long as possible, and shows the near and far zero for that path (zero at either one; the far one is more forgiving), where the bullet stays on target (from how close to how far), the maximum point-blank range, and the highest point. This zero is always the first (purple) zero box under the chart, and the chart draws its path in purple, the target band as a shaded box and a line at the maximum point-blank range Tap the circle in its box to use it for the range table and dope card. It uses the profile, gun and conditions you've entered, and doesn't include wind.

G1 or G7

Pick the BC type that matches the number you have. Many long-range bullets list a G7 number (around 0.2–0.35); it's usually more accurate past 600 yd. The Reloading recipe has the same choice and sends it over with Use in calculator.

Coriolis

With the Long chart picked, the Conditions card has a Coriolis switch. Coriolis is the earth turning under the bullet while it flies. It pushes the bullet a little right in the northern hemisphere (left in the southern), whatever direction you shoot, and a little high shooting east or low shooting west. It's tiny up close and a few inches at 1,000 yd, so it's off until you turn it on. Enter your latitude (or tap Use my location, or pick a saved range) and the direction of fire in degrees from north (0 north, 90 east, 180 south, 270 west). On a phone, Use phone compass reads it for you: hold the phone flat with its top edge pointing at the target, away from the rifle, the truck and steel benches. On an iPhone you'll be asked to allow motion and orientation access the first time. The compass gives a magnetic heading, which is close enough here. Once it's on, the Up numbers, the reticle holds, the range table (with a Coriolis column), the dope card (a Cor R column) and Field mode all include it. On a saved range, give each target its own direction (Dir °, with a compass button) and the range's latitude is used for that range's dope.

Stability and spin drift

Enter the barrel twist (1 turn in so many inches; it fills in from your gun) and the bullet length (measure one with calipers, tip to base). You then see the stability number (SG: 1.5 or more is fully stable, 1.0 to 1.5 is marginal, under 1.0 the bullet won't fly straight) and a spin drift column. If the bullet has a plastic tip (ELD-M, A-Tip, Tipped MatchKing, Ballistic Tip and the like), also enter the Plastic tip length: the tip adds length but almost no weight, so it raises the stability number and the spin drift (Courtney and Miller's correction to the Miller formula; about 0.1 to 0.4 MOA of spin drift at 1,000 yd). Measure it from the tip to where the copper starts. Makers don't publish tip lengths, so when the profile's ammo has a tipped bullet and the box is empty, a note under the stability number reminds you, with an Enter it button. With a normal right-hand twist the bullet drifts right, so hold or dial that much left on top of the wind. Spin drift is measured from your zero, the same way as Coriolis: zeroing there already took out its share.

True up the velocity

Once you've shot at long range, enter the distance and the dial that actually hit under True up velocity. It works out the muzzle velocity that matches your real drop; tap Use and the table and dope card will line up with what you saw. Use a distance well past your zero and a good group.

Weather where you are

On the Conditions card, Use the weather where I am fills in the temperature and the altitude from today's air pressure and humidity where you're standing (the altitude that gives the same air density, so humid air counts too), and tells you the density altitude, the ground's elevation and the wind. If you're within about 2 miles of one of your saved ranges that has its address, it says you're there and picks that range on the Saved ranges card. It needs a signal and Range Book's https:// address, since phones only share location with secure sites. Set the crosswind yourself, since it depends on which way you're shooting.

Print a dope card

Below the range table, Dope card makes a small card for your stock or range bag. Choose the first and last distance, how often, and whether your scope clicks in MOA or MIL (the MOA / MIL button: tap it to switch). On screen the card starts shortened and scrolls; drag the bar under it to make it taller or shorter (this device remembers), or double-tap the bar to show the whole card and again to shorten it. Printing and Field mode always show every row. It uses the zero your scope is set to, the conditions and the crosswind you entered. The card and the range table also get a shaded row at each distance where the bullet crosses your line of sight for the zero you picked: once going up (the near zero) and again coming back down (the far zero). Each is labeled zero and sits in order with the other distances; if one lands on a distance that's already there, that row is shaded and labeled instead. Tap Print dope card to print just the card (about 3½ in wide), or save it as a PDF from the print screen. On an iPhone, pinch out on the print preview to save or share it.

Field mode fills the screen with just the distance, how much to dial up and the wind hold (plus Spin R and Cor R when spin drift or Coriolis is on), in big numbers you can read at the bench. A− and A+ change the size, Bright switches to black on white for full sun, and the screen stays on while it's open (on phones that allow it). Tap ← Back or swipe in from the left to close it.

Reticle holds

The Dope card & reticle card also draws a plain reticle with a dot where the target goes. Tap any distance on the card to see it: on an iPad or computer the reticle is right beside the card, and on a phone it slides up from the bottom, with ‹ and › buttons to step to the next distance on the card. The MOA / MIL button shows the unit in use; tap it to switch. It sets both the card and the reticle. When the profile's gun has a scope (Gear & Ranges › Optics), the scope sets it (the button is greyed out) and the reticle can look like yours, or be a picture of it. Pick Hold it under Reticle: elevation to hold elevation and wind on the reticle, or Dial it, hold wind to dial elevation and hold only the wind. It uses the conditions and crosswind on the profile, and spin drift when the bullet length and twist are filled in. It isn't any brand's reticle, so count the marks on yours.

Saved ranges

Save the places you shoot under Gear & Ranges › Ranges: tap + New range, give it a name, its address, its usual temperature and altitude and any notes, and add each target with its distance, angle (up or down, in degrees) and size if you like. Changes save as you type. Under Dope, pick a Shooting profile to see the dial and wind for every target with it; the size column shows each target in MOA or MIL, so you can see how much room you have, and Use these conditions sets that profile's temperature and altitude to the range's usual ones. Each Shooting profile also has a Saved ranges card: pick a range there to see the same thing for that profile, and Edit ranges › takes you to the range. Range names show up under Where on range trips.

A range's targets are listed nearest first. If you walk or shoot them in another order, drag ⠿ beside a target to move it; the dope follows your order. Sort by distance puts them back nearest first.

A range's address and weather

Type a range's Address (a street address, or the range's name and town) and tap Find on the map. Range Book shows what it found (up to five places, each with See it on a map) and asks which one is right: tap Yes, use it or Use this one and the full address goes into the Address box; No keeps what you had. Or tap I'm here now while you're standing at it. Range Book saves the spot, the ground's elevation (and puts it in Altitude if that's empty), and an Open in Maps link for directions. Then the range's Weather card shows today's temperature, humidity, dew point, air pressure, pressure altitude, density altitude, elevation and wind there; tap Refresh for the latest. Under Dope, and on a profile's Saved ranges card, Use today's weather here puts that weather on the profile. On a range trip whose Where is a saved range with an address, the weather button gets the weather at that range (no location needed); when you start a range day near a saved range, Where is filled in for you. The address is looked up with OpenStreetMap and the weather comes from Open-Meteo: only the address or the spot's coordinates are sent, never your name or account.

Put the cards in your order

Arrange these cards, under the last card on a profile, lets you drag the cards (Inputs, Conditions, Bullet path, Point-blank range, Range table, True up velocity, Dope card & reticle, Saved ranges) into the order you want, for example the dope card first. It's one order for every profile and the Tools trajectory calculator, and the links along the top follow it. On a big screen, Inputs and Conditions keep the left column and the rest the right, each in your order. Usual order puts them back.

The inputs fold up on a phone

On a phone, when you open a profile the Inputs card folds into a one-line summary (bullet, velocity, BC, gun, zero, weather) so the results are near the top. Tap it, or the Inputs link, to open it and change anything. Every other card on a profile (Point-blank range, Bullet path, Range table, Dope card, Range trips and the rest) folds up too: tap its title to close or open it. The app remembers which ones you closed on that phone or computer, and the links at the top open a closed card for you.

Range trips

Every profile in the calculator has a Range trips log at the bottom (tap Range trips in the row of links at the top to jump there). Tap + New range trip and fill in what you like: date, where, distance, rounds fired, temperature, wind, average velocity and SD, and notes. Use the weather where I am fills in the temperature and wind, and notes the humidity, air pressure, density altitude and elevation (they're on the trip report too). If Where is one of your saved ranges with an address, the button says Use the weather at that range and uses its spot; if you're near a saved range and Where is empty, it fills it in. Import chronograph file reads the same RangeCraft, Garmin Xero, MagnetoSpeed and LabRadar files as Reloading; each string is kept with its shots, average, SD and ES, and the trip's average velocity and SD are worked out from all of them (tap Remove on a string you don't want). Add target photos and tap one to measure its groups, the same way as in Reloading; printed Range Book targets are read by themselves. Print a target for this trip opens a printable target with the trip's profile, date, distance and gun already filled in at the top. The trip list shows the best group from each trip and how many rounds you've logged. If you enter an average velocity, a button lets you make it this profile's muzzle velocity. Print trip report at the bottom of a trip opens a PDF with the details, notes, chronograph strings and target photos with the groups drawn on, ready to print or save. You don't need a reloading load for any of this, so it works just as well for factory ammo. Your Reloading photos and data stay where they are. In Chronograph, each string shows its shots in numbered boxes, the same as a group in Reloading. Type over a shot to fix it, tap + Shot to add one, or tap − Shot, tap the shots you want gone (a bad reading, an unused box) and tap Delete. The average, SD and ES update, and Undo puts them back. To type velocities in yourself, tap + Type in shots for a new string with 5 boxes.

Cold-bore shot

On a range trip, Cold-bore shot records where your first shot of the day landed from the aim point (right or left, high or low, in inches or cm), whether the barrel was clean or fouled, and the distance if it wasn't the trip's. Each gun's page has a Cold-bore log that plots every cold-bore shot in MOA and shows the average, so you can see whether your first shot tends to go somewhere other than your zero.

Transonic

Each path is drawn solid while the bullet is well above the speed of sound and turns dashed where it slows to about Mach 1.2 (transonic). Past that point drag changes quickly, the BC numbers are less reliable, and some bullets start to wobble, so treat holds out there as a starting point and confirm them on paper. A subsonic load is dashed all the way. The speed of sound depends on the temperature on the Conditions card (it's listed under the chart), so on a cold day the dashes start closer. The range table, the dope card and Field mode draw a red line between the last two distances on either side of it, and the dope card says Transonic at … under its conditions (or Subsonic from the muzzle). In Tools › Compare trajectories, a dot on each line marks where that bullet goes transonic.

Read a point on the chart

On a computer, move the mouse over a path: a small box shows the distance and how far above or below your line of sight each zero's path is there. On a phone or tablet, tap a path to see the same box; tap anywhere else to close it.

Zoom the chart

Pinch to zoom and drag with one finger to move around. A sideways pinch stretches the range, an up-and-down pinch stretches the inches. Double-tap the chart or tap Reset view to go back. On a computer, use the zoom buttons or pinch on a trackpad. Declutter hides the near and far yardage labels on the line of sight (the colored diamonds stay, and the numbers are in the zero boxes); tap it again to bring them back. The normal chart stretches the up-and-down direction a lot so you can read the drop in inches. True scale draws it at its real proportions, the same scale up and down as across, so you see how flat the bullet really flies; a 1,000 yd shot is 36,000 inches long, so even several feet of drop is a gentle curve. The up-and-down numbers switch to feet when they get big. Zooming in keeps the bullet centered and the proportions true. Tap it again to go back. Both buttons are highlighted while they're on and are remembered on this device. Drag the small bar under the chart up or down to make the chart shorter or taller (double-tap the bar to go back to the normal height). The picture doesn't stretch or squash: a taller chart shows more inches of drop and a shorter one shows fewer, so drag on a short chart to move up and down. The height is remembered on this device.

Printable targets

Under Tools › Targets (or the Tools button on Home) are targets made for Range Book. On regular Letter (8.5 × 11 in) paper: 1 big aim point, 5 aim points, and a 9-point ladder grid. On Tabloid / Ledger (11 × 17 in) paper: 1 big aim point with 1- to 4-inch rings for zeroing or long range, 6 big aim boxes, and a 12-point ladder grid. Most home printers can't print 11 × 17, but a print shop or office store can; ask for Actual size on Tabloid / Ledger paper. Bigger targets from a home printer are made of two Letter pages taped together (11 × 16 in): 1 big aim point with rings out to 5 inches, 2 big aim points with rings out to 3 inches, 4 aim points with rings out to 2 inches, and an 8-point ladder grid. Print both pages at Actual size (they print sideways), cut page 1 along its dashed line, lay it over the gray strip at the top of page 2 so the cut edge sits on the line and the grid lines meet, and tape the whole seam on the back so it lies flat. These have bigger corner squares and a small black square on each side, which is how the app knows it's a two-page target. The app tells all the sizes apart on its own when you measure a photo or use Live target. The background is a grid of 1-inch squares, and each aim point (a light red circle with a solid black center dot) sits in the middle of a square, so you can count inches by eye. The page has a 1-inch black square in each corner (the top-left one is hollow so the app knows which way is up). Tap Open PDF to print and print at Actual size (100%); the 1-inch line at the bottom should measure exactly 1 inch.

Write the charge for each aim point on its line before you shoot. Afterwards, photograph the whole page with all four squares showing, add the photo to the load, and tap Measure groups. It finds the page, sets the scale, corrects for an angled photo, and marks the holes around every aim point by itself. Aim points with no holes are left out. Check each group and pick its charge, then Save. If it doesn't find the page, tap Read printed target after a better photo, or measure by hand.

Measure sight height (height over bore)

The distance from the center of the bore to the center of the scope. It matters most at short range.

  1. Unload the gun and confirm it is clear.
  2. Find your scope tube size: 1 in, 30 mm (1.18 in), or 34 mm (1.34 in).
  3. Just in front of the receiver, measure the barrel diameter with calipers.
  4. At that same spot, measure from the top of the scope tube to the bottom of the barrel.
  5. Sight height = that measurement − ½ tube diameter − ½ barrel diameter.

3.70 in total, 30 mm tube, 0.75 in barrel → 3.70 − 0.59 − 0.375 = 2.74 in

Iron sights: measure from the top of the front sight post to the bottom of the barrel there, then subtract ½ the barrel diameter. Typical values: bolt or lever gun with low rings ≈ 1.5 in, medium/high rings ≈ 1.75–2.0 in, AR with optic ≈ 2.5–2.8 in.

Reloading

Add a load

  1. On Reloading, tap + New load. Enter the cartridge (tap Supersonic next to it to mark a subsonic load), pick the gun, and pick the bullet, powder, primer and brass from your Components (anything not saved yet can be typed into the recipe afterward). Add the Max charge from your load manual, then tap Create and plan a ladder to go straight to the ladder planner, or Create.
  2. Any group at the max charge gets an At max tag, and any group over it gets a red Over max warning.
  3. Pick the Rifle you shot it in (add guns on Gear & Ranges first).
  4. Under Ladder tests, tap + Add group in a ladder for each charge weight you test and enter the charge (or let the ladder planner make them all).
  5. Type each shot's FPS. Press Enter on the last box (or tap + Shot) to add another shot. Average, SD, extreme spread and energy fill in as you type. Groups start with 5 boxes. To get rid of some, say if you only fired 4 or a reading is bad, tap − Shot, tap each shot you want gone (they turn red and crossed out), then tap Delete. The shots after them move up, and Undo puts them back. A box left blank isn't counted either. Range trips work the same way.
  6. Enter each group's size in Group size (center to center of the two widest holes), or measure it from a target photo (below). The Distance is entered once at the top of the ladder. The MOA is worked out for you, so groups shot at different distances can be compared.

Reference

Reloading › Reference has reference lists for reloading. Pick one with the buttons at the top (Library opens Tools › Library, with every built-in list):

  • Cartridges: every cartridge Range Book knows, with its bullet diameter, maximum case length, the usual trim-to length (0.010" under the maximum), maximum overall length and primer size. Tap one for notes (like brass that takes a different primer) or to fix it for your own use. It's the same list as Cartridges in Tools › Library.
  • Bullet diameters: the cartridges grouped by the bullet diameter they actually use, so you can see which share bullets, with the common mix-ups (.308 vs .311, .355 vs .357, .452 vs .458). Tap a cartridge to open it.
  • Powder burn rates: about 250 powders from fastest to slowest, with a search box and a maker filter. Powders you have under Components are marked. It shows roughly where a powder sits; never use it to pick a substitute powder or a charge.
  • Pressure signs: what each sign on the ladder checklist looks like, what it means and what to do.
  • Glossary: reloading terms from annealing to work hardening, with a search box.

Range Book remembers which list you last looked at on that phone or computer.

Reloading notes

Reloading › Notes is for anything that isn't about one load: die and press settings, what to order, ideas to try, a powder that's back in stock. Tap + New note, give it a title if you like (otherwise its first line is the title) and type. It saves as you go. Pin a note to keep it at the top, search them from the box above the list, and delete one from the bottom of the note (with an Undo). Notes are private and are included when you export your data.

Develop and Load

Each load has two views, switched at the top. Develop is for working it up: the recipe, ladder tests, ladder planner, summary, charts and target photos. Load is the finished load as a load sheet you can't edit: the charge and powder, bullet, primer, brass, trim length, COAL, bullet diameter, your manual's max and the gun, with the velocity and best group at that charge, Use in calculator, and Loaded rounds for logging batches. To change anything on it, go back to Develop.

When your groups show what works, tap This is my load next to that charge in the Summary, or use Create the load at the bottom of Develop. That charge becomes the working charge: the load opens on Load from then on, and the charge is filled in for you when you log a batch, add the load to your ammo, work out the cost per round or send it to the calculator. To pick another, use Ready to load it? on Develop again.

Turn on Locked (on Develop) once a load is done. That locks the whole Develop page (recipe, groups, photos, sharing) except Ready to load it?, which moves to the top of the page so you can still pick a different working charge. A locked load can't be deleted, updating a component under Components leaves it alone, and you can still log batches on Load. Turn Locked off to make changes.

In the recipe, a bullet, powder, primer or brass picked from Components shows as one tinted line with its details. The bullet's weight, length, diameter and BC come from the saved bullet, so you change them in one place (under Components, then tap Update there). Tap Change to pick a different one or type it in, and Done to fold it back to one line.

Finding your way around a load

The buttons under a load's name (Recipe, Summary, Charts, Targets, Ladder tests) jump straight to that part of the page. Once a load has velocities, its recipe folds up into a one-line summary; tap Recipe to open it again.

Inventory

Every bullet, powder and primer under Reloading › Components has an On hand amount (count for bullets and primers, pounds for powder) and a Warn when level. On a reloading load, the Loaded rounds section (the Loaded link at the top) logs each batch you load: how many rounds, the charge, the brass lot and the date. Logging it takes the bullets, primers and powder (rounds × charge) out of inventory (a ladder test does the same with Take components out of inventory), as long as the recipe uses saved components with an amount filled in. Remove on a batch puts them back. Anything that drops below its warning level shows as Low on the Components list and on Home.

Cost per round

Each component also has a Cost section: what you paid and for how many (a box of 100 bullets, an 8 lb jug of powder, a brick of 1,000 primers). For brass, the price is spread over how many times you expect to load each case (5 if you leave it blank). The Loaded rounds section on a load then shows what each round costs, with the bullet, powder (at the charge you enter), primer and brass broken out, and each batch you log keeps its total cost.

Brass lots

Under Reloading › Components › Brass, add a lot for each batch of cases you keep together. Enter how many cases, how many times they'd been loaded before Range Book, and when you last annealed and trimmed them (Annealed today and Trimmed today fill in the date). Each batch you log with that lot adds one to its load count. The old 5.56 → 300 Blackout headstamp notes are folded up at the bottom of the Brass list; tap them to open.

Components: bullets, powders and primers

Reloading › Components keeps the components you use: bullets (maker, name, the caliber as sold like 38 Special or 30 cal, the actual diameter like .357 used for the math, weight, BC, BC type, length), powders, primers and brass lots. Tap + Add bullet (or powder, or primer) to open the list Range Book knows, the same way + Add scope works: a search box at the top, the list in tiles grouped by maker (bullets by caliber, primers by size), and + Enter a … yourself for one that isn't listed. Ones you've already saved aren't shown again. Add the … from my loads fills the list from recipes you've already entered. Powders: about 150 popular ones from Hodgdon, IMR, Winchester, Alliant, Accurate, Ramshot, Vihtavuori and Norma (type a name, maker or kind, like "h4350" or "alliant ball"); picking one fills in the maker, name and kind (ball, extruded or flake) for you. Primers: 46 from CCI, Federal, Winchester, Remington, Fiocchi and Murom, with their size. Bullets: about 1,000 from Berger, Hornady, Sierra, Nosler, Barnes, Speer, Lapua, Berry's, X-Treme and CamPro, grouped by caliber. The plated and cast ones show the cartridge they're sold for, so "380 100" or "9mm plated" finds them. Search with the caliber, weight and type, like "6.5 147 eld", "30 175 smk" or "berger hybrid" (nicknames such as SMK, TMK, ELDM, ABLR and LRHT work). Picking one fills in the maker, line, caliber, diameter, weight, BC (G7 when the maker publishes one, otherwise G1) and length, and its notes say where the numbers came from. Makers change their BCs from time to time, so check them against your box. Berry's, X-Treme and most CamPro handgun bullets have no published BC; type one in if you need it for the calculator. The same names are suggested as you type a powder into a recipe, and a listed name fills in its maker. If you change a saved bullet, powder or primer later (a corrected BC, a new name), its Loads card marks the loads that still have the old details; tap Update to copy the new details into them, along with any reloaded ammo made from them. A recipe that's out of date also shows Update this recipe under that component. Inside a load, the Components › button at the right end of the shortcut bar takes you straight to Components, with a ‹ Back to button to return to that load. The recipe's Brass can be picked from your saved brass lots the same way; it fills in the brass and its case length (add a Case length to the lot under Components), and makes that lot the default when you log a batch. COAL stays with each load, since it depends on the bullet and seating depth.

In a recipe, pick a saved component from the shaded box above the Bullet, Primer or Powder fields; it fills in the details for you (for a bullet: weight, BC, length and diameter too). You can still type everything by hand. If you type one that isn't saved yet, a Save to Components button appears so you can keep it for next time. Cartridges you type are remembered too, and the cartridge and maker boxes suggest what you've used before as you type.

Ladder tests

A load's groups live in Ladder tests. Each ladder (Ladder 1, Ladder 2 and so on) is one batch you loaded and shot, kept separate from the others. At the top of each ladder are its Loaded date, Tested date, Temperature (°F) and Distance, entered once for the whole ladder. Each ladder can have its own distance, and every group in it uses that distance for its MOA. Under them are its groups, one per charge, then its target photos. Inside a ladder, + Add group adds another charge, and Import chronograph file as new group brings in velocities as new groups in that ladder. Delete ladder removes the ladder and its groups (with an Undo). Tap a ladder's title to fold it down to its title and summary line, and tap again to open it; each phone or computer remembers which ones you folded.

Once you've loaded a ladder, tap Take components out of inventory under its dates. It works like logging a batch: one round for each shot box at each charge, so it takes that many bullets and primers, plus the powder for every charge, out of your Components. Pick the Brass lot you used and that lot's load count goes up by one. The ladder then shows what it took. Put them back undoes it, say if you change the ladder and want to log it again. Ladder rounds aren't added to your ammo inventory, since you shoot them for the test. Deleting a ladder doesn't change your inventory, so tap Put them back first if you never loaded it.

To start another ladder, tap Plan a new ladder at the bottom of Ladder tests, or + Empty ladder to set up the groups yourself. Your first ladder stays as it was. When a load has more than one ladder, the Summary and Velocity by charge show one ladder at a time (the newest to start); pick another, or All ladders, from Showing at the top of them. Tap Combine matching charges to see each charge once, with every shot at that charge from all your ladders pooled: the average velocity, SD and ES come from all of them, and the group is the average of the groups you measured at that charge. Your ladders and their shots aren't changed; tap it again to go back.

Plan a ladder test

Under Ladder tests, tap Plan a new ladder. Enter the first charge, the step and the last charge (it starts with your manual's max) plus how many shots per charge. It shows every charge first, flagging any over max, then Create ladder makes a new ladder with a group for each charge, ready for your chronograph import. (On a brand-new load, it fills the empty Ladder 1 instead of adding a second one.)

The planner has a Distance, a Loaded date (today to start) and a Tested date you can leave blank until you shoot. They go at the top of the new ladder, where you can change them later.

To label the box of ladder rounds, tap Print a label in the planner (or Ladder label in a ladder once its groups exist; it uses that ladder's charges and dates). One 3.5 × 2 in label holds the recipe and every charge, numbered in order with a box to tick as you load each one, plus shots per charge, distance, the loaded date and the tested date (or a blank line to write it on).

Velocity by charge

Once two or more groups have charges and shots, the Velocity by charge chart plots average speed for each charge, with a bar showing ± one SD. Look for a flat spot where adding powder barely changes the speed: that's usually the most forgiving charge. Under the chart, the fps gained per grain between each step is listed. The dashed red line is your max charge. Groups with a size also get a purple diamond showing their MOA on the right-hand scale, so you can see which charge shot tightest.

Pressure signs

Each group in a ladder has Pressure signs: tap any you saw on that charge's cases or bolt (flat or cratered primers, ejector marks, a heavy bolt lift, sticky extraction, loose primer pockets), and enter case head expansion if you measure it. A charge with any of them gets a ! triangle on the Velocity by charge chart and a pressure signs tag in the Summary, and they're listed in the Excel and PDF exports. This is a notebook, not a pressure gauge: pressure can be dangerous with no visible signs at all, so always stay within your load manual.

Import from your chronograph

Set up a group for each charge weight in the ladder first. Then tap Import chronograph file on the ladder's first group and pick the export from your RangeCraft (.xlsx), Garmin Xero (ShotView .csv or .xlsx) MagnetoSpeed (LOG.CSV from the V3's memory card, or the .csv from the XFR app) or LabRadar (the SR0001 Report.csv files from its SD card; pick several at once and each series fills its own group, SR0001 first). Each string fills the next empty group in that ladder in the order you shot them (Range Book puts the strings in time order, since some chronographs, like Garmin's, list the newest first). If you named each string with its charge weight on the chronograph (like "25.9gr N140"), it goes straight to the group with that charge instead, wherever it is in the ladder. If the ladder has no tested date yet, it takes the date from the file when the file has one (MagnetoSpeed's memory-card file doesn't, so set that date yourself). Check that each string landed on the right charge weight. If the chronograph caught a bad reading (a miss or an echo), tap − Shot, tap that shot and tap Delete.

Range Book checks every string as the velocities come in, from a file or typed in, here and on range trips. A shot that's way off from the rest of its string (a chronograph misread, an echo or a typo, like 1,312 in a string of 2,800s) turns red, with a note saying it might not be correct. Check it against your chronograph, fix the number, or delete it with − Shot. It only flags shots far outside the string's normal spread (needs at least 3 shots), so an ordinary flyer isn't marked. Tools › Chronograph import check marks them too.

Target photos

Each target photo belongs to the ladder you shot it with. Tap + Photo in that ladder (or next to the ladder's name on the Targets card) to take a picture or choose one. The Targets card shows the photos under each ladder, and each ladder shows its own photos too. Tap a photo to see it full size, add a caption, delete it, or move it to another ladder with Shot with. When you measure groups on a photo, you pick from that ladder's charges. Photos added before ladders existed are linked for you when the app can tell which ladder they go with; open any that say Pick a ladder and choose one.

To keep a copy of a target photo, open it and tap Download photo (the picture as taken) or Download with marks (with the measured shots and groups drawn on it). On a phone it opens the share sheet, so you can Save Image to your photos, save it to Files or send it; on a computer it downloads.

Measure groups from a photo

One photo can hold several groups, each with its own aim point and charge weight. Measuring gives you two sizes: the group size (center to center of the two widest holes) and the mean radius, the average distance of every hole from the group's center. Mean radius uses every shot, so it's a steadier way to compare charges, especially with small groups. Both show on each group and in the Summary, along with how far the group's center is from your aim point (for a zero check). Typing a group size by hand clears the photo's mean radius, since it no longer matches.

  1. Tap a target photo, then Measure groups.
  2. Scale (once per photo): tap two points a known distance apart, such as two grid lines 1 inch apart, and enter that distance in Scale (in). Check Distance (yd) too.
  3. Aim: tap the first group's aim point.
  4. Box: drag a box around that group's shots. It tries to mark the holes inside. Entering Shots fired first helps; it fills in from the charge's chronograph shots when it can.
  5. Shots: check every mark. Tap a wrong one to remove it, tap a missed hole to add it, drag a mark to move it. Holes that touch usually need adding by hand. Pinch to zoom.
  6. Under This group is, pick the charge weight it goes with.
  7. Tap + Group for the next group and repeat from the aim point. Tap a group's chip (or any of its marks) to go back to it.
  8. Tap Save. Each matched charge gets its group size, distance, mean radius and where the group's center landed from the aim point, and the group MOA shows on the Velocity by charge chart.

Group size is center to center of the two farthest shots, the same as calipers across the outside edges minus one bullet width.

Live target (phone on a spotting scope)

Range Book can watch a printed Range Book target through your phone's camera and mark each shot as it lands. Put the phone on the spotting scope with an adapter so it holds still, and aim the scope so the whole page and all four corner squares are in the picture. It needs Range Book's https address (the camera doesn't work on a plain http address).

The camera doesn't have to be straight on. Live target uses the corner squares to work out how the paper is tilted and measures every shot on the flattened target, so the group size and MOA are right from off to the side too. Up to about 30° makes no real difference, and 30° to 45° works well (zoom in a little). From 45° to 60° the holes look like thin ovals, so touching holes are harder to tell apart. Past about 60° it often can't find the corner squares at all. You don't have to guess: once it finds the target, Live target works out the angle and shows a note on the camera picture from about 45° and a red warning from about 60° (an iPad watching it shows them too). It counts tilting up or down the same as side to side. Keep the paper flat: staple or tape all four corners. The ⓘ next to Camera off to the side? in Tools › Live target says the same.

  1. In a ladder, tap Live target (next to + Photo). From a range trip, use Live target next to + Add target photo. To use it without a load, open Tools › Live target.
  2. Allow the camera. On a phone with more than one back lens, it uses the main lens so it doesn't keep jumping between lenses up close to the eyepiece; pick another under Camera lens if you like (it's remembered on that phone). Through a spotting scope the page often looks gray and washed out; Range Book allows for that, but zoom the scope so the page fills more of the view if it can't find the corner squares. When it finds the four corner squares it says Target locked and zooms in on aim point 1. It still watches the whole page, and widens the view by itself if a shot lands outside the zoom. Tap Whole target (or the small picture in the corner) to see the whole page, and Zoom to aim to go back.
  3. Check Charge for this aim, Shots and Distance.
  4. Fire, then tap Shot. It compares the page with how it looked before the shot and marks the new hole, numbered, with the group size, MOA, mean radius and where the group's center is from the aim point. A hole in the black center counts too.
  5. If it misses a hole, tap the hole on the picture to add it. Tap a wrong mark to remove it. Undo takes back the last change.
  6. After the last shot for that aim point it shows the group. Tap Next to move to the next aim point and charge, or use ‹ Aim and Next aim › any time.
  7. Tap Save when you're done. It saves one photo of the target with every group measured, the same as Measure groups, and each charge gets its group size, mean radius and distance. You can open the photo and edit the marks later. (From Tools, it's kept under Tools › Live target › Saved until you move it to a range trip or a ladder.)

Not a Range Book target? Live target works on any paper or board. Tap Not a Range Book target? on the camera picture, tap the target's four corners (top-left first, then clockwise), pick or type its size, then tap each aim point in the order you'll shoot them and tap Done. Without the corner squares it can't follow the target if the phone moves, so keep it still; if it does move, tap Tap corners again. Your marks stay put.

Your reticle over the target: turn on Show my reticle on the Live target screen, then pick the Shooting profile for the gun you're shooting. From a range trip it uses the trip's profile on its own (its gun, scope and selected zero). Range Book draws that scope's reticle (your own reticle picture if you've added one) over the camera picture, to scale for the Distance you entered, with the mark you'd hold for that distance on the current aim point, so you can see where the crosshair sits and how your shots land against the reticle. The hold uses the profile's zero; type a different one in Zero if your scope is zeroed somewhere else (leave it blank to use the profile's). It also includes the profile's wind, spin drift and scope power, the same as the reticle on the dope card, and if the profile is set to Dial it it tells you how much to dial. Your choices are remembered on that phone.

Leaving a phone at the target (for long range, with Remote on another phone at the bench): the screen stays on while Live target is open. On an iPhone, Turn on Range Focus runs a shortcut you make once that turns on a Focus, so calls and notifications don't interrupt it (tap the ⓘ next to it for the steps). Android web apps can't do that by themselves, so Silence calls shows how to turn on Do Not Disturb in two taps. If something still interrupts the camera, Live target starts it again by itself and finds the target again, and your marks are kept; if the Remote connection drops, the phone starts it again and the watching device follows it. Set the phone's screen lock to Never (Auto-Lock on iPhone, Screen timeout on Android), keep it on a battery pack, and test it with a call and a text before you walk down range.

Bigger picture on a phone: drag the bar under the camera picture down to make it bigger; the buttons and numbers below it then scroll. Drag it up to make it smaller, or double-tap the bar to fit everything on the screen again. It's remembered on that phone.

Or start it on your iPad, with the phone as its camera: on the phone, open Tools › Live target and tap Be the camera for your iPad, aim it at the target and leave it (the screen goes dark after 30 seconds to save battery; tap it to see the camera). On the iPad, start Live target the usual way (from a ladder, a range trip or Tools › Live target) and pick Use the iPhone on the scope. The phone starts by itself with that setup: the ladder's charges, the distance and shots, and the trip's Shooting profile for the reticle. The iPad has the Shot, Undo, Aim and Save buttons, Listen for shots with the iPad's own microphone, and Show my reticle with its profile and zero. Save puts the target where you started it on the iPad. To change guns, loads or profiles, tap ← Back on the iPad (it offers to save the shots first), then start Live target again from the new place: the phone goes back to waiting in between and keeps its camera open, so you never have to touch it.

Control it from your iPad (or any phone, tablet or computer signed in to your account), so you don't touch the phone on the scope: on the phone's Live target screen, tap Remote. On the iPad, open Tools › Live target and tap Watch. The iPad shows the phone's screen, updated about twice a second, with the group numbers, and its Shot, Undo, Next aim, Whole target and Save buttons work the phone. Tapping a hole on the iPad's picture adds or removes a mark on the phone. Both need a signal to reach your Range Book (an iPad on the iPhone's hotspot counts). Keep the phone's screen on. Tap Remote again on the phone to stop sharing; nothing from it is kept.

Listen for shots uses the microphone: each loud bang counts as a shot, so you don't have to tap Shot. Turn it on only when nobody is shooting near you, because their shots count too. The bar next to it shows how loud the last sound was, and the white mark is how loud a shot has to be. Pick a Sensitivity: Normal for an unsuppressed rifle, Suppressed for a rifle with a suppressor (still loud, but less of a crack), or Quiet .22 for a suppressed .22 or subsonic loads. If your shots don't reach the mark, pick the next one. The more sensitive it is, the more other noises count, so use the least sensitive one that hears every shot. It remembers your choice.

It works best in good, even light. At long distances a phone may not see small holes clearly; add them by tapping. Keep the phone and scope still: if the page moves a lot, wait a moment for it to find the corners again.

Shot by shot: which shots were fast or slow

When you shoot a ladder with Live target, it remembers the order of the holes. Once that group has its chronograph velocities (typed in or imported, in the order you fired), the group shows Shot by shot: each shot's velocity next to where it hit, and a small chart of height against velocity. It tells you whether faster shots hit higher (or lower), and by how much per 10 fps, so you can see how much of your up-and-down spread comes from velocity. If a hole or a velocity is missing the pairs shift, so check that the chronograph caught every shot. Editing the marks in Measure groups keeps the order.

Use a load in the calculator

In a load's Summary, tap Use in calculator on a group. It makes a new Shooting profile with that bullet weight, average velocity, the ballistic coefficient from the recipe, and the sight height of the gun you picked. Anything missing, fill in on Shooting.

Other tools

  • Duplicate recipe copies a load without its shots, batches or working charge, handy for a retest. Pick a different powder or bullet there to start working up a variation.
  • Your brass headstamp ratings are under Reloading › Components › Brass, folded up at the bottom.
  • Shot velocities are whole numbers. A decimal you type is rounded when you leave the box.

Share a load

Open the load and tick people under Sharing. They can see the load, its velocities and photos but can't change anything. Untick to stop sharing. Loads shared with you appear under Shared with me; use Duplicate recipe to make your own editable copy.

Back up, export and import

Tap More › Account (or Account at the top on a computer). Download backup saves everything in your account in one .zip file, photos included. Download Excel and Download PDF are for reading and printing (the PDF includes your target photos).

To bring data back in, or move it to another Range Book, use Import on the same page and pick a backup or an Excel export (Excel files don't carry photos). Importing adds to your account: anything already there is left alone and nothing is deleted, so importing the same file twice doesn't double anything.

Super admin: the first admin on a Range Book is its super admin (marked on the Admin page). Other admins can't delete, turn off, remove as admin, rename, reset the password of, or download the data of that account, so someone you make an admin can't lock you out. Only the super admin can download or restore the whole site, and only they can hand the role to another admin: on that person's card tap Make super admin twice. You stay an admin afterwards. The super admin can't remove their own admin without handing the role on first.

The whole site (super admin): on the Admin page, Download site backup saves every account and everything in it (data, photos, videos and files; document vaults stay locked) in one .tar.gz file on the device you're using. Keep it somewhere other than the server. To bring a whole site back, set up a fresh Range Book (an empty data folder), sign in with the account it asks you to make, and on the Admin page tap Choose backup file, pick the file and tap Restore twice. Every account comes back with its own password, so then sign in with your old account. It also takes a .zip of one of the nightly backup folders. It only works on a fresh install, so it can never wipe out a Range Book that's in use.

Encrypting site backups (super admin, optional): on the Admin page under Encrypt site backups, type a passphrase of 12 or more characters twice and tap Save passphrase. From then on every site backup you download, by hand or with the nightly copy, is locked with it (the file ends in .enc), and Restore the whole site asks for it. Range Book can't recover a lost passphrase, so keep it in a password manager. If you change it or turn it off, backups made before still need the passphrase they were made with. Leave it off if you don't want encrypted backups.

Nightly copy to another computer (super admin): if Range Book runs somewhere else, like a cloud host, your home server can download the whole site every night. On the Admin page under Nightly copy to another computer, tap Turn on. Copy the backup key and the ready-made script it shows (they're only shown once). On Unraid, install User Scripts from Apps, add a script, paste it in, change DEST to the folder you want, and set it to run daily. It keeps the newest 30 and says FAILED if a download doesn't work. The Admin page shows when the key was last used. Anyone with the key can download everything, so if it gets out, tap Make a new key (the old one stops working) or Turn off.

Import from a spreadsheet

To add a lot of gear at once, tap Account › Import from a spreadsheet (or Import from a spreadsheet on the Gear & Ranges and Components lists). Download the template gets an Excel file with a tab each for guns, optics, lowers, uppers, barrels, factory ammo, bullets, powders, primers and brass, with drop-down lists for cartridges and other choices, and a tip on columns like Twist when you click a cell. To bring in a gun built from a lower and an upper, list them on the Lowers and Uppers tabs, then on the Guns tab fill in its Lower and Upper columns (Manufacturer and Model can stay blank; it's named after the lower, and its specs come from the upper). Several rows with the same lower become one gun with several uppers. On the Optics tab, Kind says whether it's a Scope, Red dot, Holographic or Prism sight (blank is a scope); a red dot or holographic sight needs only Dot size, Ring and Magnifier, not the scope columns, and On gun puts it on the gun with that name. On the Barrels tab, On gun is the complete gun the barrel goes on. They can name gear that's already in Range Book or a row in the same file. Fill it in with Excel, Numbers or Google Sheets, save it as .xlsx (or a single tab as .csv), and pick it with Choose a file to import. Your own spreadsheet works too: Range Book matches the columns by their headings (Make and Model are joined into a gun's name, S/N is the serial number, and so on).

Nothing is saved until you tap Import, and before then it asks about anything it isn't sure of: a column it doesn't recognize (pick what it is, add it to Notes, or leave it out), a cartridge, BC type, primer size or scope it doesn't know (pick the right one, or keep it as typed), a number or date it can't read (fix it, or leave it blank), and anything already in Range Book (the same gun by serial number or name, the same scope, ammo or component). For those it shows what's different and you pick Skip, Update it (only the boxes filled in on the spreadsheet change) or Add as new; rows that match exactly are left alone. Download it with my gear filled in gets a copy of everything you have, so you can fix things in the spreadsheet and import it back as updates.

Gear & Ranges

Guns

The Gear & Ranges tab lists your guns under Guns. The list is grouped by type: rifles, then pistols, then shotguns. Tap the star on a gun to make it a favorite: favorites are listed first, under ★ Favorites, and come first in Home's Most used guns and when you start a range day (a gun's page has the same star at the top). Put them in your own order: press and hold one (or drag it with a mouse) and drag it up or down the Favorites list. Tap + Add gun or tap a gun to open it, fill in its Manufacturer and Model (the gun is listed and picked everywhere by the two together, like Tikka T3x Lite), pick its Type (Rifle, Pistol or Shotgun; when you fill in the cartridge first, Range Book guesses it, and you can tap another), then fill in the Cartridge it's chambered for, its serial number, barrel, twist rate, sight height and notes. Under Photos, tap + Add photos to keep pictures of the gun; the first one shows in your list of guns. Gun photos and serial numbers are private to you, and the serial numbers are included when you export your data, which is handy for insurance. To export just your guns, tap Export Excel or Export PDF at the top of the Guns list: the spreadsheet has one row per gun (serial number, barrel, twist, round count, barrel life, cleaning), and the PDF has a summary table, then a page for each gun with its details, notes and photos. Each gun's page also lists the Reloading loads, Shooting profiles and range trips that use it; tap one to jump to it. When a load has a gun picked, Use in calculator also brings that gun's sight height across.

Nickname: give a gun a name of your own (like Elk rifle) in the Nickname box at the top of its page. It's used everywhere the gun shows up: the lists, Shooting profiles, range trips, the dope card, Home and the exports. The manufacturer and model still show under it in the Guns list. Leave it blank to use the manufacturer and model. A gun with several uppers shares one nickname, with each upper's cartridge after it.

Lowers, uppers and built guns

For ARs and other guns made of a lower and an upper, add each part under Gear & Ranges › Guns › Lowers & uppers. A lower has its manufacturer, model and serial number, with no caliber. An upper has its cartridge, barrel length, twist, sight height and scope. Then put a lower and an upper together to make a gun: tap + Add gun and choose A lower + an upper under Made as (or tap Make a gun with this lower or upper on either one), and pick them. The gun takes the upper's specs and the lower's serial number, and you can rename it. Put more than one upper on the same lower and they become variations of one gun: the Guns list shows it once, with a chip for each upper's cartridge (tap a chip to open that one), and its page has an Uppers row to switch between them, plus + Add upper to add another. The gun's name is shared by all of them, and each variation is shown as the name plus its cartridge (Aero Precision M4E1 · 300 Blackout; when two uppers have the same cartridge, the barrel length or the upper's name tells them apart). Each variation keeps its own type, notes, photos and loads. On Shooting and Reloading the gun picker groups the variations under the gun's name, and Start a range day asks which upper you're shooting. The Upper list starts each upper with its cartridge and is sorted by it, so you can tell them apart. In the Guns list, a lower that's already in a gun and a barrel that's on a gun are shaded, so the ones still free stand out.

Each lower and upper keeps its own round count (and uppers their barrel life), from the range trips and load-development groups shot with any gun built with it. Trips and ladders remember the lower and upper they were shot with, so if you change a gun's upper later, old rounds stay where they were. The gun's own count includes everything shot as that gun.

Barrels

Swap barrels on a complete gun? Add each one under Gear & Ranges › Guns › Barrels (or + Add barrel on the gun's page) and pick the gun it goes on. Each barrel can have its own cartridge, length, twist, sight height and scope; leave a box blank to use the gun's. You can move a barrel to another gun, and its round count goes with it. When you pick a gun that has barrels on Shooting, Reloading or Start a range day, Range Book asks which barrel you're using, or The gun as it is, and uses its specs. Trips and ladders remember the barrel, and each barrel keeps its own round count, barrel life and cleaning reminder.

The guns export has a Lowers uppers barrels tab, and each gun shows what it's built from.

Cartridges

Cartridges in Tools › Library shows the whole list: search it, or tap Rifle, Handgun or Rimfire. It's for reference only, so don't trust it over your gun's barrel stamp, a current load manual and the SAAMI drawing. Tap a cartridge to change any of its numbers or names if you find a mistake: a changed box turns your accent color and says changed, with Revert to … to put the original back (or Revert all changes). Tap + Add a cartridge for one that isn't listed (a wildcat, say); yours are listed under Yours with a ✕ to delete them. Your changes and additions are used everywhere in Range Book and sync to your other devices.

Range Book knows about 115 rifle, handgun and rimfire cartridges. Wherever you enter a cartridge (a gun, a reloading recipe, factory or reloaded ammo, a Shooting profile), start typing any name for it, like 3006, 308 Win, 7.62 NATO or 6.5 CM, and pick it from the list. It's saved under its standard name (30-06 Springfield, 308 Winchester and so on), so loads group together, and the bullet diameter fills in if it's empty. Under the box you'll see the bullet it takes and the SAAMI (or C.I.P.) maximum case length and overall length. A cartridge that isn't in the list (a wildcat, say) can still be typed in; just enter the bullet diameter yourself. Cartridges you'd already typed with another name for a listed one were switched to its standard name.

Warnings: Range Book checks that things fit, and warns you (it doesn't stop you) when they don't:

  • A Shooting profile whose ammo isn't right for its gun gets a warning at the top and a Check cartridge tag in the list. So does a reloading recipe whose gun is chambered for something else.
  • Some ammo is safe in another chamber but not the other way around, and Range Book knows which: 38 Special in a 357 Magnum, 223 Remington in a 5.56 NATO (both in a 223 Wylde), 44 Special in a 44 Magnum, 45 Colt in a 454 Casull or 460 S&W, 32 H&R and 32 S&W Long in a 327 Federal, 22 Short and Long in a 22 LR, 280 Remington in a 280 Ackley Improved, and others. The reverse (357 Magnum in a 38 Special gun, 5.56 in a 223-only gun) is flagged as dangerous, and so is 300 Blackout with a 5.56/.223 gun. Ammo whose bullet is bigger than the barrel's bore (8mm Mauser in a 30-06, say) is flagged as dangerous too.
  • A few combinations get a Check first note instead of a block: 308 Winchester and 7.62x51mm NATO (check your gun's manual), 9mm NATO in a 9mm Luger gun (SAAMI lists it as unsafe because it's loaded hotter, but many makers allow it), and +P or +P+ ammo, which is only for guns their maker rates for it. Type +P with the cartridge (38 Special +P) and Range Book keeps it.
  • A bullet whose diameter doesn't match the cartridge (a .308" bullet in a 7.62x39, say), a case length over the maximum, and a COAL longer than the SAAMI maximum (common when seating close to the lands, so make sure it fits your magazine and chamber).

Always confirm against your gun's barrel stamp and a current load manual: this list is a check, not a replacement for them.

Round count and barrel life

Each gun's page has a Round count. It adds the rounds from range trips on Shooting profiles that use that gun, the shots in your load-development groups on Reloading loads that use it, and the Rounds before Range Book you enter. Fill in Barrel life to see a bar of how much is used (it turns red at 80%, and Home warns you). Set Clean every and tap Cleaned today after cleaning to see the rounds since then; Home tells you when it's due. When you fit a new barrel, set Barrel fitted on to that date and Rounds before Range Book to 0.

Optics

Gear & Ranges › Optics keeps your scopes. Each scope and suppressor has a Picture at the top of its Details: tap + Add picture (or Replace picture, or Remove), and it shows on the list. A scope's picture is separate from the picture of its reticle. Tap + Add scope and search the list of about 130 popular scopes (type a maker, a model, or MIL or MOA) to fill in the power, focal plane, units, click value and reticle name from the maker's published specs, or tap + Enter a scope yourself. Most of the list also has the reticle's mark spacing (how far apart the main marks and the smallest marks are, like marks every 1 MIL, 0.2 between), and on a second focal plane scope the power the marks are true at; picking one of those sets Range Book's plain reticle to match, so you don't have to with Change how it looks. For many it also sets the general layout: holdover dots as a grid or a tree (or none), and an open center or a center dot. It's still Range Book's own plain reticle, not the maker's drawing. Drop-chart (BDC) and plain duplex reticles don't have evenly spaced marks, so they keep the standard look. Scopes with a bullet drop reticle say so on the list and on the optic's page: its marks won't line up with the even marks Range Book draws, so use the maker's chart to see which mark matches a hold, or upload a picture of your reticle. When a model comes with more than one reticle, the spacing is for the first one listed. Check the click value against your turrets (a few makers don't publish it, so it shows as Not published until you pick yours).
