If your turrets aren't in the same units as the reticle (a MIL reticle with MOA turrets, say), set Turrets: the dope card then dials in the turret's units and the reticle holds stay in the reticle's. Put it on a gun with On gun on the scope's page, or with Scope on the gun's page (a gun has one scope). Every Shooting profile that uses that gun then takes its MOA or MIL from the scope, so the dope card's Scope clicks in switch follows it, and the scope's name goes on the card.

Red dots and holographic sights

Red dots, holographic and prism sights go in Gear & Ranges › Optics with your scopes. Tap + Add optic and search: the list has about 75 popular red dot, holographic and prism sights as well as the scopes (type red dot to see only the sights), with their dot size, ring, click value and mount. Not listed? Tap + Red dot, + Holographic or + Prism (or change Kind at the top of an optic's page). The Optics list is split into Scopes, Red dots and holographic sights, and Prism sights, and any optic can have a Nickname: when it's filled in, it's the name you see everywhere. A red dot or holographic sight has its maker, model, serial number, Dot size in MOA, the Ring around it if it has one (like a 65 MOA ring or a 68 MOA EOTech ring), a Magnifier if you run one behind it, and its click value (only used for zeroing). Put it on a gun with On gun, and set the gun's Sight height: the distance from the center of the bore to the center of the dot.

A red dot has no turrets to dial, so on a gun with one the dope card changes: Hold says how far above (↑) or below (↓) the target to put the dot, in inches (cm in metric), and Hold (dots) says the same in dot widths, to the nearest quarter (with a 2 MOA dot, 1½ dots is 3 MOA). Center means hold right on it. Wind is in inches too. The MOA / MIL switch and the dial choice go away. Tap a distance and the picture beside the card shows the dot over the target, to scale, with a sentence like "Put the dot 7.9 in above the target". Field mode and printing use the same columns, and Live target's Show my reticle draws the dot. A prism sight works like a fixed-power scope, with its reticle in MOA or MIL.

Second focal plane scopes have marks that are only their true size at one power, often the highest (the scope's manual says). Enter it in Marks true at power. On the dope card's reticle a Scope power picker then works out the hold in marks for the power you're on; at the true power it's the same as the MIL or MOA.

Make the reticle look like yours

Range Book's reticle is a plain one, not any brand's design. Tap Change how it looks (on the scope's page, or under the reticle on the dope card) to open a window with a preview where you pick where the main marks are, the small marks between them, the holdover dots (a full grid, a tree that widens as it goes down, or none), the numbers, the center (lines that meet, an open center, or an open center with a dot) and the line thickness. Back to the standard look undoes it.

A target behind the reticle

Under the reticle on the dope card, Target behind it puts a target in the scope view: a 4, 6, 8, 10 or 12 inch circle, a 2/3 IPSC silhouette, or a pronghorn, coyote, deer, elk or prairie dog. It's drawn life size for the distance you picked on the card (and for the power you picked, on a second focal plane scope), so you see how big it really looks. The animals are life-size silhouettes facing left, with their vital zone (heart and lungs, just behind the front leg) marked with a dashed ring. The Gray and Color buttons next to the menu switch the animals between plain gray and their natural colors; Range Book remembers which you like. In Hold it mode the target sits on the mark you hold; with Dial it, hold wind it sits on the crosshair, moved over for the wind. Your own reticle picture works too: Range Book makes its light background see-through so the target shows behind the lines.

Your own reticle picture

For your exact reticle, use a picture of it. On the scope's page, under Reticle, pick A picture of my reticle and tap + Upload a picture: a straight-on picture of just the reticle, like the drawing in the scope's manual or on the maker's website (a screenshot is fine). Then set its scale: tap the exact center of the crosshair, tap a mark on the line a known distance away (the farther the better, like the 5 MIL mark), and enter that distance. If the scope came from the Library, the window tells you how far apart its marks are, which mark to tap and fills in its distance, so you don't have to look it up. + zooms in so you can place them exactly, and Center or Mark lets you move one. Tap Save, and the dope card puts the dot on your own reticle. The best picture is the maker's drawing of the reticle on a white background; a photo through the scope works too if you point it at something bright and even (a white wall or an overcast sky) at full power with the reticle sharp. The picture is private to you and is in your backups. Set the scale redoes it, and Remove picture goes back to the plain reticle.

Ammunition

Gear & Ranges › Ammo keeps the ammo you shoot, in two lists: Reloaded ammo and Factory ammo. Each one counts the rounds you have on hand (loaded or bought, minus what your range trips fire) and can warn you when you're running low.

Subsonic ammo: the button next to Cartridge says Supersonic; tap it and it changes to Subsonic (tap again to switch back). Do the same on a reloading recipe, next to its Cartridge. Subsonic recipes and ammo get a Subsonic tag in the Reloading and Ammo lists, and so does any Shooting profile that uses that ammo. Reloaded ammo made from a recipe follows the recipe's setting.

Reloaded ammo

Each batch in the batch history has a Label button (and one appears right after you log a batch): it shows a label with the load name, bullet, powder and charge, primer, brass lot, COAL, velocity, date and round count. Pick how many copies and tap Print labels; they print 3.5 × 2 in (business-card size), ten to a page, on plain paper or Avery 5371/5376-style card stock or labels.

To compare loads, tap Compare loads at the top of the Reloading list and pick up to three. A table shows the components, the working charge (or the last one used) with its velocity, SD, ES and group, the best group and lowest SD at any charge, cost per round and rounds loaded. The lowest SD, ES, group size and cost are highlighted. Tap a load's name to open it.

To keep count of rounds you've loaded, open a recipe on Reloading, switch to Load and log a batch in Loaded rounds. The first batch at a charge adds the load to your ammo inventory, copying the bullet, BC, powder, primer and brass from the recipe and the velocity from your groups at that charge. Each later batch at the same charge adds to the count, removing a batch takes it back off, and range trips with it count it down. The card shows how many you have on hand, and the batch history folds away underneath. You can also start one from Ammunition → + Reloaded ammo: pick a recipe, or choose None: I'll pick the parts myself, then pick the bullet, powder, primer and brass from your Components and fill in the charge. Each part shows its details underneath (weight, BC, diameter, kind, case length, on hand, cost); tap Edit to change them on the Components page, then ‹ Back to to return. + Create new at the top of each list makes a new component and opens it so you can fill it in. An entry can also be linked to a recipe later with Fill in from this recipe. Once you've loaded it, turn on Locked at the top so the recipe (name, cartridge, bullet, powder, charge, primer, brass and COAL) can't be changed by accident, not even by an Update from Components; the rounds, velocity and notes stay editable. Duplicate at the bottom makes an unlocked copy (with no rounds yet) to start a new one from. The cost per round comes from the prices on your components, or type it in. Use in calculator makes a Shooting profile from it, just like factory ammo.

Factory ammo

On Gear & Ranges › Ammo, tap + Add ammo. It works like adding a scope: a search box, the factory loads in tiles grouped by cartridge (smallest bullet first), + Enter factory ammo yourself, and + Reloaded ammo to make an entry from one of your Reloading recipes. Type a cartridge, maker or weight to narrow it down. There are about 155 popular loads in 56 cartridges, from 17 HMR to 50 BMG (Hornady, Federal, Sig Sauer, Remington, CCI, Speer, Nosler and Barnes; rifle, rimfire and handgun) with the bullet, BC and box velocity already filled in from the maker's published data (Nosler and Barnes velocities come from gun-shop listings instead, with the BC from the makers' bullet data); tap one to add it to your list. Not listed? Tap + Enter factory ammo yourself on the same screen and fill in the maker, cartridge, bullet, weight, BC, the velocity on the box (and your measured velocity if you've chronographed it), plus rounds bought, price and lot number. Use in calculator (pick the gun first if you like) makes a profile on Shooting with those numbers. You can also pick the ammo in a Shooting profile's Ammunition box. Tap it to open a short list: your reloaded ammo, your factory ammo, and the catalog loads for that load's cartridge. Type in its search box (a maker, powder, bullet weight or cartridge) to search everything, including the whole catalog. Picking a catalog load fills in the numbers and adds it to your Ammunition for you. The range trips you log on that profile count down your rounds on hand (bought minus fired), and + Bought more adds a new box. Set Warn when fewer than and Home tells you when you're running low. If your range trips have average velocities, it offers to use their average as your measured velocity.

Sharing factory loads

Entered a factory load that isn't in the catalog? Open it and tick Share this load with everyone on this Range Book (it isn't there if an admin has turned sharing off under Admin › Community sharing). It shares the maker, product, cartridge, bullet, weight, BC, diameter, box velocity and its box photo; your rounds, price, lot, measured velocity and notes stay private. Changes you make later update the shared copy, and unticking it (or deleting the ammo) removes it. Shared loads show up under their cartridge on the + Add ammo screen, shaded and marked SHARED with the person's name so you can tell them from the maker's data; tap one to add it to their own list. You can remove your own shared loads there, and admins can remove any of them. If someone's account is deleted, the loads they shared (and their box photos) stay for everyone, listed as shared by a former member.

Box photos

Open any factory ammo and tap + Add a photo of the box. A quick phone snap is fine; it's shrunk before it's saved. If the ammo came from the catalog, the photo is shared with everyone on this Range Book, so the next person can tell at a glance it's the right box, and it shows next to that load in the catalog. (An admin can turn that sharing off under Admin › Community sharing; then everyone's box photos are private, and loads can't be shared either.) Photos of ammo you entered yourself stay private. You can delete your own photos; admins can delete any shared photo that doesn't match (there's a list of them all on the Admin page).

The tabs along the top are Guns, Optics, Suppressors, Magazines, Ammo, Inventory, Ranges and Notes. On a phone the row scrolls sideways.

Suppressors

Add each suppressor under Gear & Ranges › Suppressors with its maker, model, caliber rating, serial number and the date the tax stamp was approved. Tap + Add suppressor for the list of about 430 suppressors, grouped by maker the same way as scopes (type a maker, model, caliber, "rimfire" or "full auto"), or + Enter a suppressor yourself. + Add a suppressor… on a gun's page opens the same screen and puts the new one on that gun. Picking one fills in the maker, model and caliber rating, and puts the maker's published length, weight, diameter, mount, full auto rating, barrel-length minimum and other limits in its notes. Those limits also show under Details. Check them against your can's manual, since makers change ratings between versions. If it lives on one gun, pick that gun under On gun (or pick the suppressor on the gun's page, like a scope); it's then filled in on that gun's new range trips. If it moves between guns, leave it off: each range trip has a Suppressor box where you pick the one you shot, and you can always change it there. The trip's rounds count toward that suppressor, so each one keeps its own round count (add Rounds before Range Book for what it had already seen), with a cleaning reminder like a gun's. Its page lists the range trips shot with it.

Rated for suggests cartridges and size families as you type: pick a family like 30 caliber, 22 rimfire or 6.5mm if the maker rates it for any bullet up to that size, or a cartridge like 5.56 NATO if it's rated for just that one. Range Book then checks it against the gun's cartridge on the suppressor, on the gun and on each range trip. A bullet wider than the rating gets a red Don't shoot warning, since it can hit the baffles. A rimfire suppressor on a centerfire cartridge, or a pistol suppressor on a rifle cartridge, gets a Check first note to look at the maker's manual. A suppressor on a gun it isn't rated for is also flagged on the Suppressors list. The check only goes by bullet size and type, so the manual's other limits (barrel length, full auto, mount) still apply.

Suggestions you've typed before (gun makers, magazine makers and models, inventory categories, trip places, your own cartridge names) drop down as you type. Tap the × next to one to take it off the list, for a typo or something you don't have any more. Your saved gear doesn't change, and it comes back if you type it in again.

Magazines

Gear & Ranges › Magazines keeps each magazine as its own entry, so you can tell which one is causing trouble. Give each a Mag #: the number or mark you put on it with a paint pen or tape (1, 2, A, red tape). Add its maker and model (mags of the same maker and model are listed together, with how many you have), capacity, which guns it Fits, its Cartridges (a mag can take several: an AR-15 mag might take 5.56, 223 and 300 Blackout; tap × to remove one, tap one of your guns' cartridges to add it, or search for another, and ticking a gun under Fits adds its cartridge), where it's kept and photos. + Add another like this copies the type, cartridge, capacity and guns to a new mag with the next number. When a mag jams, fails to feed or doesn't lock the slide back, tap + Log a problem on that mag with the date and what happened; the list shows how many problems each has. Tick Retired to keep a bad one in the list, greyed out. For a group of identical mags, Set guns for all next to the group's name ticks or unticks a gun on every mag in it at once (a dash means only some are marked). Each gun's page has a Magazines card (tap its title to fold it) listing the mags that fit it, with + Add a magazine for this gun. To bring in a list, use the Magazines tab of the import spreadsheet (Account › Import): How many makes that many numbered mags from one row, and Fits takes your guns' names and Cartridges takes one or more cartridges, each separated by commas.

Inventory

Gear & Ranges › Inventory keeps track of the rest of your gear. + Add supplies is for things that get used up (batteries, target pasters, earplugs, patches and solvent, hand warmers): give it a count and Warn when at or below, and use − 1 used and + 1 to keep the count right. + Add equipment is for things you keep (a chronograph, rangefinder, bipod, magazines, cases) with a serial number, price, date bought and photos, handy for insurance. Either can have a category, where it's kept, a gun it goes with and a Check or replace by date that can repeat (a battery every year, a hunting license, a first-aid kit). Low supplies and dates within two weeks are listed first under Needs attention, and on Home. When you've done it, tap Done and a repeating date moves to the next one.

Gear notes

Gear & Ranges › Notes is for notes about your gear that don't belong to one gun: where things are stored, a gunsmith's work, part numbers, warranty details. Tap + New note, give it a title and type. Add Pictures and Files (PDFs, manuals, receipts, spreadsheets, up to 20 MB each) to a note. Notes save as you type, Pin to the top keeps one first, and the search box looks through titles and text.

The vault needs Range Book's https address (or localhost on the server itself): browsers don't allow encryption on a plain http page, so over http the vault cards say so instead.

Tick Lock in the vault to encrypt a note: its title, text, pictures and files are locked on your device with your vault passphrase before they're saved, and its pictures and files move into the vault. Nobody can read it without the passphrase, not even the server's admin. Until you unlock the vault, the list just shows Locked note and searching skips it. Untick it to take the note back out of the vault (Range Book asks first). Pictures and files on a note that isn't locked are private to you but not encrypted.

Document vault

Suppressors, guns and inventory items have a Documents card for papers like a tax stamp, a receipt or a manual (PDFs or pictures, up to 15 MB). The first time, tap Set up the vault and choose a vault passphrase. It isn't your sign-in password: use something long you don't use anywhere else, like four or five random words. Every document is locked (encrypted) on your phone or computer with that passphrase before it's uploaded, so the server only ever holds scrambled data. Nobody can open your documents without the passphrase: not the person who runs this server, not an admin (even one who resets your password), not someone with your backup file, and not Range Book's maker. That also means a forgotten passphrase can't be recovered, and neither can the documents, so keep the originals somewhere too.

To see or add documents, tap Unlock and type the passphrase. On a computer Open shows the document in a new tab; on a phone it unlocks it, then a second tap opens the share sheet to view, print or save it. The vault locks itself after 15 minutes, when you tap Lock, or when you close Range Book. Account › Document vault shows how many documents you have and lets you change the passphrase (your documents stay as they are). Your backup file includes the vault, still locked: restoring it brings the documents back, and they open with the same passphrase. One caution: whoever controls the server could, in theory, change Range Book's code to capture a passphrase as it's typed, so only use the vault on a Range Book run by someone you trust.

With no signal: in More › Account › Document vault, turn on Keep on this device for offline use on each phone or tablet you want it on. That device then keeps a copy of your vault, still locked with your passphrase, and updates it whenever you open the vault with a signal. With no signal, the Documents cards say they're using that copy: unlock with your passphrase as usual and open your documents. Adding or deleting documents still needs a signal. Turn the switch off to remove the copy; signing out removes it too.

Tools

Tools (a tab on a computer, or More › Tools on a phone, or the Tools button on Home) holds quick calculators, one tile each with a line about what it does. Tap a tile to open that tool, and ‹ Tools (or swiping back) to return to the tiles. To put the tiles in your own order, press and hold one and drag it where you want it (on a computer, just drag it; with a keyboard, Alt + the arrow keys move the selected tile). The order is saved to your account, so it's the same on every phone and computer; Put them back in the usual order under the tiles undoes it. Nothing in Tools is saved: change a number and the answer updates.

  • Library: every list built into Range Book: bullets, cartridges, powders, primers, factory ammo, scopes and suppressors, with how many of each (the Built in Library card on Home and Library in Reloading › Reference open it too). Tap a list to look through it, grouped by maker or caliber, with a search box. Tap anything in it to see all of its numbers. If one is wrong (a maker's new BC, a typo), fix it right there: the box you changed turns your accent color and says changed, the entry is marked Edited, and Revert to … (or Revert all changes) puts the maker's number back. Your fixes are only for you, sync to your other devices, and are used the next time you add that entry, from the Library or from any + Add screen. Things you've already added are your own copies and keep their own numbers; change those on their own pages. Search edited to find the ones you've changed. + Add to my … on an entry adds it to your Components or Gear and opens it. Cartridges is the cartridge list described under Cartridges, and the bottom of the Library links to the other reloading reference lists.
  • Compare trajectories: up to six bullets on one chart, all with the same zero, sight height, temperature and altitude. Type each one's weight, velocity and BC, or fill it in from a Shooting profile, your ammo or the factory catalog. Switch the chart between Path (above or below your line of sight), Dial (MOA or MIL to dial up), Wind (drift in a 10 mph crosswind), Speed and Energy, and between Short, Medium and Long (200, 400 or 1,000 yd). The table under the chart has each bullet's numbers. Each line has its own color and dash pattern, so they're easy to tell apart in Red Night too. It remembers your bullets on that phone or computer; Reset starts over.
  • Chronograph import check: pick your chronograph's export to see how Range Book reads it before you import it: each string's shots, average, SD, spread and time, in the order they were shot, and which ladder charge it would go to when its name has a charge. Nothing is imported or saved. If a file doesn't read right, this is the screen to show when you report it.
  • Trajectory calculator (also the Trajectory calculator button on Home): the whole Shooting calculator without making a profile. Pick a gun and ammo (your own, or anything from the factory catalog, which here only fills in its numbers) or type the bullet weight, velocity, BC and sight height, and every card works the same as on a profile: conditions and wind, bullet path and zeros, point-blank range, range table, true-up, dope card and saved ranges. Nothing is saved to your profiles; this device remembers the last numbers so it opens where you left off. Reset clears it for new numbers (Undo brings them back), and Save as a Shooting profile keeps it as a profile, so it gets range trips too, and opens it on Shooting.
  • Stability: will a bullet be stable in your barrel's twist? Pick a Bullet from your Components and a Gun (for its twist) side by side, or type the numbers in. On a Shooting profile, Check barrel twist (under Inputs) opens it filled in from that profile. It shows the Miller stability number (1.5 or more is fully stable, 1.0 to 1.5 marginal, under 1.0 the bullet will likely tumble) and the slowest twist that fully stabilizes that bullet. Colder air and lower altitude make the number smaller, so check it for the coldest day you'll shoot.
  • MOA/MIL: turn a group size or hold into MOA and MIL at a distance, or an angle back into a size.
  • Powder: how many rounds a container of powder makes at your charge, what the powder costs per round, and how much you need for a number of rounds. Fill in from uses a Reloading load's charge and, if its powder has a price in Components, the price.
  • Convert: grains and grams, fps and m/s, inches and millimetres, yards and metres, foot-pounds and joules. Type in either box.
  • Hit chance: your odds of a first-round hit on a target at a distance. Pick a Shooting profile (it uses its trajectory and conditions), the target size, and what throws the shot off: your 5-shot group size, your velocity SD, and how far off your wind call and range could be. It shows the chance, a picture of the likely spread on the target, what would help most (a perfect wind call, a tighter group…), and the same target at other distances. On a Shooting profile, Hit chance at a distance under the dope card opens it for that profile.
  • Live target: the spotting-scope camera without a profile, load or range trip. Set the bullet diameter, distance and shots per aim point, tap Start Live target, and use it the same way (see Live target under Reloading). Save keeps the target photo and its measured groups in your Range Book, listed under Saved on that page (with no signal, it waits on the phone and uploads later). Tap a saved one to see it, fix its marks with Edit measurement, or bring it into a range trip or a reloading ladder with Move to. A range trip also has + Saved Live target. After saving, Share picture gives you a picture with every group drawn on it and its size, MOA, mean radius and center underneath, to keep in Photos or send to someone. Saved Live targets are in your backups too.
  • Cartridges: the cartridge list Range Book uses for bullet diameters and its warnings, with each one's SAAMI maximum case length and overall length, trim-to length and primer size (also under Reloading › Reference) and what else is safe in that chamber. It's for reference only. Fix anything you find wrong (changed boxes are colored, with Revert) or add your own; Cartridges (in the Gear & Ranges help) has more.
  • Targets: the printable targets (see Shooting above).

On a Shooting profile with a bullet length and twist filled in, a warning also appears at the top when the bullet isn't fully stable in that twist under today's conditions, with a Check it in Tools button.

The fine print

Shooting is dangerous.

Guns are loud, fast and unforgiving. Gunpowder sitting in your garage is too. You knew that, but the lawyers in my head insisted.

This is a notebook, not a load manual.

Range Book is a log and a calculator built by a guy who likes to shoot. It is not a load manual, a gunsmith, or your mom. Every charge weight in here is just a number somebody typed, and somebody makes typos. That includes the max-charge warnings, the ladder test planner and anything someone shared with you. Check every load against a current published manual from the powder or bullet maker before it goes in a case. Start low, work up, and watch for pressure signs. If your primers look like pancakes, stop.

The math is an estimate.

Trajectories, dope cards, true-up, spin drift, the weather and group measurements are all educated guesses. Confirm your dope on paper before you bet a shot or a hunt on it. Nothing here tells you whether a shot is safe; that's on you. Know your target and what's behind it.

Software breaks.

There may be bugs. Data may get lost. Back up anything you care about (Account › Download backup).

The part where you agree.

You're responsible for your own guns, ammo, components and decisions. If you do something dumb, like blowing up a rifle, hurting yourself, hurting someone else, or putting a hole in something you didn't mean to, that's on you. It's not on the person who runs this site or anyone who helped build it. Range Book comes with no warranty of any kind, express or implied. If you can't live with that, close this page and go read a reloading manual. (You should probably do that anyway.)

Follow the four rules, wear eye and ear protection, and keep the powder away from the cigarette.

Limits

Range Book uses a 3DOF point-mass solver, like most phone and web ballistic calculators. It treats the bullet as a point that slows down and drops, with drag from your BC on the standard G1 or G7 curve at the bullet's speed compared with the speed of sound. It includes air density from temperature and altitude (today's weather fills in an altitude that also allows for pressure and humidity), powder temperature (when you've entered or learned its sensitivity), uphill and downhill angle, crosswind, and spin drift from the twist and bullet length.

With the Long chart you can also turn on Coriolis (the earth turning under the bullet), which is added to that same point-mass path; it's still a 3DOF solver. It leaves out the bullet's own wobble and stability in flight. The 6DOF models that track that need measured data for each bullet. Most bullets lose stability and slow down unevenly as they near the speed of sound, so treat numbers past that point as estimates, especially with a marginal twist. A bullet's real drag also differs a little from the standard curve, so the further out you go, the more the drops can drift from what you see. Always confirm your drops on paper at known distances.

Two conventions worth knowing. BCs are taken as ICAO standard-atmosphere values (59°F, 29.92 inHg, dry air), the way Berger, Hornady and most modern makers publish them; older Sierra-style G1 numbers were measured against slightly thinner "Army Standard Metro" air and will show about 0.3 MOA more drop at 1,000 yd here than in a calculator built on that standard. Uphill and downhill shots use the usual cosine rule (only that share of the drop counts), which is within 0.1 MOA of the full answer to 600 yd at 30°, and about 0.5 MOA at 1,000 yd. The range table stops where a slow bullet's path gets steeper than 45°, because a table by distance stops meaning anything there.

What throws the shot off

Group size is the usual 5-shot extreme spread (rifle, ammo and you together). "Give or take" is how far off your wind or range could typically be: 2 mph is a good wind call, 5 mph a tough day; a laser rangefinder is within a yard or two. Each is treated as a normal spread, so take the answer as a guide, not a promise.

Put your phone on a spotting scope (an adapter keeps it still) and aim it at a printed Range Book target with all four corner squares in view. After each shot, tap Shot and it marks the new hole and updates the group. Save keeps the target and its groups in your Range Book (listed under Saved, below), so you can add it to a range trip or a ladder later, and Share picture gives you a picture with every group and its numbers.

Camera off to the side? It's fine: Live target corrects for the angle.

It needs Range Book's https address: phones only allow the camera on a secure address. Listen for shots (on the Live target screen) uses the microphone instead of the Shot button; use it only when nobody is shooting near you.

Guest access

Guests can use everything without an account, but nothing they enter is saved and they can't see anyone's data. Any number of people can be guests at once.

Community sharing

On: a photo of a box of catalog ammo is seen by everyone here, so the next person can tell it's the right box, and people can tick Share this load with everyone on factory ammo they entered themselves. Off: everyone sees only their own box photos, new ones stay private even if you turn sharing back on later, shared loads are hidden from + Add ammo, and nobody can share a new one. Photos and loads that were already shared are hidden, and come back if you turn it on again. On a big public server, off is safer: someone will eventually add the wrong box or the wrong numbers.

Shared photos people have added (you see them here even with sharing off, so you can clean up). Delete any that don't match the load or shouldn't be there.

A copy of everyone's data and photos is saved every night on the server, in the backups folder inside Range Book's appdata folder. The last 14 days are kept. To restore one, see the README.

Downloading or restoring the whole site is up to the super admin, .

Download the whole site

One file with every account and everything in it: data, photos, videos and files (document vaults stay locked). Keep it somewhere other than the server, like your computer or cloud storage.

Download site backup

Encrypt site backups (optional)

Off: a site backup is a plain .tar.gz that anyone holding the file can open. On: every site backup you download (here and with the nightly copy below) is locked with a passphrase you choose, and Restore the whole site asks for it. Range Book only keeps a key made from the passphrase, never the passphrase itself, and can't get it back if you lose it: without it, those backups can't be opened. Keep it in a password manager. Backups in the server's own backups folder aren't changed.

Nightly copy to another computer

Lets another computer, like a home server, download the site backup on a schedule without signing in. It uses a backup key instead of a password. Anyone with the key can download everything on this Range Book, so keep it private, and make a new one (or turn it off) if it gets out.

Restore the whole site

Brings back everything from a site backup: every account (with its password), all the data and all the files. It only works on a fresh install, so it can't wipe out a Range Book that's in use.

Users

The super admin is the first admin, unless they've handed it on. Other admins can't delete, turn off, demote, rename, reset the password of, or download the data of the super admin, so nobody you make an admin can lock the owner out. Only the super admin can hand the role to another admin (Make super admin), and they stay an admin afterwards.
